en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question on Inference.

4. The Question on Faults in the Practice “Venerable Nāgasena, when the Bodhisatta performed austerities, was there no such exertion, no such striving, no battle against the defilements, no crushing of the army of Death, and no regulation of food as there was in this [present] practice? Was it not of such a kind?”
Having found no satisfaction whatsoever in his exertion and having allowed that very mind to decline, he said:
"Indeed, by means of this bitter practice of self-mortification, I do not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Could there be another path to enlightenment? Then, becoming disenchanted with that, he attained omniscience by means of another path.
Furthermore, he instructs and exhorts his disciples in that very practice:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth!
Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
"Shake off the army of Death,
as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut!
"But by what reason, venerable Nāgasena, does the Tathāgata instruct and exhort his disciples in that very course of practice from which he himself has become disillusioned and detached?"
“Even then, Great King, as it is now, that very same practice was followed; by following that very practice, the Bodhisatta attained omniscience.
However, Great King, while the Bodhisatta was exerting extreme effort, he completely cut off his food.
Due to that cessation of food, weakness of mind arose in him.”
Because of that weakness, he was unable to attain omniscience. However, by consuming only a moderate amount of solid food and following that very same practice, he attained omniscience before long.
That, O Great King, is the very same practice for all Tathāgatas to acquire the knowledge of omniscience.
Just as, O Great King, food is the support for all beings, and all beings experience happiness depending upon food; so it is with this practice.
In the same way, Great King, that very same practice leads all Tathāgatas to the attainment of omniscient knowledge.
It is not, Great King, the fault of the exertion, nor of the striving, nor of the battle against the defilements, by which the Tathāgata at that time did not reach omniscient knowledge;
rather, it was solely the fault of the cessation of nutriment, which occurred constantly.
"This path is indeed prepared.
Great King, suppose a man were traveling along a road with excessive speed; he might then become exhausted, or perhaps he were a cripple unable to walk upon the surface of the earth.
Now, Great King, is there any fault in the great earth because that man became exhausted?"
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
The great earth is always prepared, venerable sir; what fault is there in it?
That man’s own effort is the fault, by which he was struck down.”
“In the same way, Great King, this was not the fault of the undertaking, nor of the exertion, nor of the battle against the defilements,
by which the Tathāgata at that time did not attain omniscient knowledge; rather, it was solely the fault of the cessation of nutriment,
for this path had always been prepared.”
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to wear a soiled garment and would not have it washed; that is not the fault of the water, for the water is always ready.
That is the fault of the man alone.
Even so, Great King, this is not the fault of the undertaking, nor of the exertion, nor of the battle against the defilements. By whom...
“At that time, the Tathāgata had not yet attained omniscient knowledge; rather, this was simply the fault of the cessation of food.
This practice has always been prepared; therefore, the Tathāgata instructs and exhorts his disciples by means of that very same practice.
Thus, Great King, that practice is always prepared and blameless.”
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the fourth question, concerning the fault in the practice.
